newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ABN, ING get takeover ammunition from NY listing.
newsitem.headline: ABN, ING get takeover ammunition from NY listing.

text.p: ABN AMRO and ING Groep, the two largest Dutch banking and insurance companies, are gathering ammunition for further acquisitions in the U.S. through their New York Stock Exchange listings this month.

Analysts say the U.S. share market debuts would give the acquisitive duo shares which can be used for acquisitions in the United States, eliminating the tax liability which has to be paid for cash takeovers.
"Sellers are more interested if you use shares because there's no tax liability on them," said Hans Pluijgers of Kempen and Co
U.S rules preclude companies using foreign stock in acquisitions.
Bart van der Feen of IRIS said ING, which lists on June 13, could afford to spend seven to eight billion guilders ($3.7-4.2 billion).
"I am expecting a very big acquisition in the U.S. life (insurance) market before the end of the year," he added.

ABN AMRO, which lists in New York on Wednesday, is one of the biggest foreign banks in the United States, where it has built a beach-head in the mid-west, while ING is a major player in the U.S. insurance industry.

But ING has long been interested in buying a large U.S. life insurer to give itself the critical mass to compete against rivals such as Aegon NV, which recently bought Providian Corp's insurance operations for 3.5 billion.
Aegon, which is already listed in New York, used its own shares to pay for the business.
Analysts do not expect ING to empty its warchest all in one deal.
ING missed out on an opportunity last year when it tried to buy U.S. insurer First Colony, later sold to GE Capital.
The listings continue the remarkably similar developments of ABN AMRO and ING, both formed through mergers in the early 1990s and forced to expand outside their small home market.
Analysts said both companies had increased the efficiency of their domestic operations through post-merger cost cutting but needed acquisitions to maintain the momentum in earnings growth.

ING is also keen to expand its securities distribution business in the United States, having pulled out of talks last week to buy Wall Street investment bank Dillon Read & Co, which was then sold to SBC Warburg.
Analysts believe ING is more likely to make the next big U.S. takeover as ABN AMRO is still digesting its recent $1.9 billion takeover of Michigan-based Standard Federal Bank Inc.

Analysts said both groups wanted to broaden their shareholder base, particularly to U.S. pension funds which can only invest in U.S. listed shares. U.S. investors hold only nine percent of ABN AMRO shares while U.S. and Canadian investors hold 13 percent of ING.
BZW analyst Heinie Hakker said the two Dutch groups were prepared to list in New York because they were more comfortable about complying with U.S. GAAP accounting standards.
U.S. rules require greater financial disclosure than Dutch rules. The key element was the decision by both groups earlier this year to reveal the size of their hidden reserves.
The reserves, built up over time as the banks overprovided for loan losses, amounted to 4.02 billion guilders for ABN AMRO and 2.55 billion guilders for ING, both at December 31.
"It was always an obstacle. They were rather secretive about that," Hakker said.
ABN AMRO, the largest bank in the Netherlands, this month issued a prospectus for a small capital raising which is accompanying its listing.

The document, more detailed than it provided in the past because it had to meet stringent U.S. GAAP accounting rules, included the first breakdown of divisional profits and revealed that the value of doubtful loans fell in the last two years although the balance sheet continued to grow.
"That's one of the reasons why everybody is buying Dutch banks ... because the quality of the loan portfolio is extremely healthy," said Van der Feen.
But analysts were looking forward more to ING's prospectus for details of previously-undisclosed gains on the group's huge investment portfolio.
In a preliminary prospectus issued earlier today, ING said it realised gains of 885 million guilders on sales of shares and convertible debentures in 1996, up from 178 million in 1995.
